stories.title: A ribbon-shaped cloud on Mars may form without any dust to seed it, a modeling study suggests
paragraphs: NASA's Astronomy Picture of the Day for Nov. 2, 2026 features the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud, a long water-ice cloud on Mars that NASA says was first recorded by Viking Orbiter 2 in 1977 and has since been imaged in more detail by ESA's Mars Express spacecraft; the featured image is from 2018. According to APOD, the cloud forms only in spring and summer and only in the morning, and wind carries it downstream from the Arsia Mons volcano into a tail that can stretch more than 1,500 kilometers.

Science News reported on Oct. 29 that researchers, in a study published Oct. 7 in Nature Geoscience, propose that the cloud forms through homogeneous nucleation, meaning without dust or salt particles to seed it. Science News notes that this way of forming clouds was thought to be possible on paper but not to occur naturally. The cloud forms daily in the same spot, roughly 45 kilometers high on the volcano's slope, for several months each year, the outlet reports.

According to Science News, the team could not reproduce the cloud with computer models that use standard cloud physics, said François Forget of the Laboratoire de Météorologie Dynamique (LMD) in Paris. Planetary physicist Jorge Hernández-Bernal, who did the work at LMD, said few dust particles stay suspended high in the thin Martian atmosphere. In the team's model, air flowing across the volcano rapidly lifts a moist parcel of air that expands and cools until it holds 100,000 times more moisture than it can hold, and that excess quickly forms ice crystals.

Science News reports that the model does not perfectly match satellite observations. Samuel Atwood of the University of Maryland, Baltimore County and NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, who was not involved, told the outlet it is "a pretty compelling story" but "only one view or one perspective on it," and that future measurements would add certainty. Hernández-Bernal said he plans to test alternative explanations.

image.credit: ESA, DLR, FU Berlin; processing by J. Cowart, via NASA APOD
image.alt: Mars Express view of the long, thin Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud stretching across the Martian surface

stories.title: Melting permafrost has produced a new type of large landslide, in which whole slabs of still-frozen ground thaw from below and slide downhill
paragraphs: A huge 2018 landslide in Canada's Northwest Territories represents a new class of catastrophic landslide that researchers call a permafrost detachment slide, Science News reported on Nov. 2, describing a study published Sept. 28 in Geophysical Research Letters. According to Science News, a slab of earth roughly equal in volume to seven Great Pyramids of Giza suddenly slid downhill, even though it began in frozen ground that had been held in place for years. The slide dammed the Redstone River in the Mackenzie Valley and created a 3.5-kilometer-long lake.

Permafrost geologist Joseph Young, who was based at the University of Alberta at the time, told Science News that permafrost traditionally melts from the top down and releases a muddy slurry, but at some sites in the region large blocks of still-frozen ground seemed to have moved hundreds of meters. His team studied the two largest such slides: the 2018 event, which moved 18 million cubic meters of earth, and a 2017 event that moved 4.5 million cubic meters. Field observations showed that both began along flat sliding surfaces about 20 meters underground, at the base of the permafrost layer, and satellite data showed the ground at both sites had been creeping meters each year for decades.

The team tracked ground temperatures from 2020 to 2022 at undisturbed forest sites and at sites burned by wildfire about 25 years earlier, then ran computer simulations of how the ground changes after a fire. According to Science News, the researchers concluded that wildfire and extreme summer heat can warm and weaken the frozen surface so it starts creeping and forms tension cracks. Water can then seep down through those cracks to beneath the permafrost, thawing it from below until it detaches.

Young said more than 150 other slides in the region, identified from satellite observations, may also have been permafrost detachment slides, and that they could happen wherever there is a relatively thin, warm permafrost layer and a rapid warming event. "This is a direct reality of a changing climate," he told Science News. Dmitry Nicolsky, a permafrost geophysicist at the University of Alaska Fairbanks who was not involved in the study, said the work shows scientists need to study what is happening beneath the surface, because "we don't know how [the ground] will move — it might go slowly or it might go catastrophically."

image.alt: The 2018 permafrost detachment slide that dammed the Redstone River in Canada's Mackenzie Valley

stories.title: Webb finds unusually heavy hydrogen in the methane of interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS, pointing to a very cold birthplace
paragraphs: The interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS carries methane that is unusually rich in heavy hydrogen, according to a study published in Nature Astronomy and reported by Phys.org on Nov. 1. Using the James Webb Space Telescope, Nathan Roth of American University and NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center and colleagues measured a ratio of heavy to ordinary hydrogen in the comet's methane of about 3.2%, roughly 13 times as high as in comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko, which likely formed in our own solar system. "This D/H ratio exceeds any other value for methane measured in the solar system," the authors write.

Heavy hydrogen, or deuterium, has an extra neutron in its nucleus, and swapping it into a methane molecule changes the molecule's infrared signature, Phys.org explains. Webb observed the gas cloud around the comet's icy nucleus on Dec. 22 and 23, 2025, when 3I/ATLAS was about 2.4 times as far from the sun as Earth is. The team modeled and subtracted light from other gases, then picked out the much fainter traces of the deuterium-bearing methane. Comet 67P is the only other comet in which that form of methane has been detected, and that measurement needed a close-up visit by the Rosetta spacecraft.

According to the report, extremely cold gas, around 10 degrees above absolute zero, favors chemistry that builds deuterium-rich ice on interstellar dust grains. The methane's ratio was about three times the ratio previously measured in the comet's water, and the researchers suggest the methane may have formed later, after the chemistry had more time to concentrate heavy hydrogen. The team argues the result fits a proposed origin in a cold cloud or the surroundings of a forming star, with relatively few elements heavier than helium and heavy cosmic-ray bombardment.

Phys.org notes that this is a plausible history rather than a pinpointed birthplace. Direct measurements of methane's deuterium ratio in distant star-forming regions are lacking for comparison, and the few chemical models that estimate it fall short of the value measured in 3I/ATLAS, so the comet now gives those models a demanding test.

image.alt: Chart comparing deuterium-to-hydrogen ratios in solar system and extrasolar sources, including 3I/ATLAS

stories.title: NASA's Swift observatory is expected to fall back to Earth within days, and experts say only small fragments should survive
paragraphs: NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is expected to crash back to Earth in the next few days, Space.com reported on Nov. 1. The telescope will re-enter the atmosphere in an uncontrolled fashion after a robotic rescue mission failed to boost it to a higher orbit. Swift launched in November 2004 and spent two decades studying gamma-ray bursts and other cosmic events with three telescopes: a Burst Alert Telescope, an X-Ray Telescope and an Ultraviolet/Optical Telescope.

According to Space.com, NASA reported on Oct. 20 that Swift's orbit had decayed to 171 miles (275 kilometers) and that the roughly 3,300-pound (1,500-kilogram) observatory could no longer compensate for the increased drag. It entered safe mode, and its operations team at Pennsylvania State University then sent a command that effectively ended its operations. Space.com says it is not yet clear exactly when or where Swift will come down.

Darren McKnight, a senior technical fellow at the tracking company LeoLabs, told Space.com that Swift will likely break up enough on re-entry not to pose a ground casualty hazard, though internal parts of its X-ray and optical telescopes might survive. Aerospace engineer Dean Sladen of Accu Components told the outlet that the most likely survivors are Swift's six heavy reaction wheels and tougher telescope parts such as lenses and mirrors, that its mask of around 52,000 small lead tiles will almost certainly melt, and that Swift's orbit only passes over a band within about 21 degrees of the equator, which is mostly ocean.

Sladen said no detailed risk assessment for Swift's fall appears to have been published, while noting that NASA's orbital debris rules cap the risk of human casualty at one in 10,000. Space.com reports that NASA has said harm to anyone on the ground is unlikely and that LeoLabs also describes the risk as very small. McKnight said there are now 10 times more objects re-entering each year than five years ago.

stories.title: DeepSeek open-sources dsh-superagent, a research prototype of a coding agent that waits to be asked and splits work into parallel sessions
paragraphs: DeepSeek published a public GitHub repository, deepseek-ai/dsh-superagent-prototype, on Oct. 31, 2026, under the MIT license. The README describes dsh-superagent as a proactive coding agent for one GitHub repository, packaged as a bundle for DeepSeek Harness. It listens to GitHub and, optionally, the Feishu chat app, and when someone who is allowed asks it for work, it opens a work item, works on it in its own agent session and directory, and answers in the original conversation, for example with a pull request. A web panel shows what needs a person.

The README labels the code a research prototype for reference only and not an official DeepSeek product. It says much of the engineering was done by coding agents, that it may still contain bugs, and that it differs from DeepSeek's internal version and from the design described in its post Exploring Super-agent Design: Towards a More Autonomous Agent System, some of which is not implemented. The stated principle is to take as little human attention as possible and give as much value as possible, so the agent acts only when asked or when a rule the team wrote allows it.

MarkTechPost reported on Nov. 1 that the design uses two layers: a long-running Router that handles interaction and dispatch, and isolated Worker sessions that do the work, one per work item, which the project calls a Ticket. It reported that unrequested work is gated by three modes, off, observe and auto, with observe as the default, in which the agent only records what it would have accepted. MarkTechPost listed the requirements as Node.js 22.19 or newer, git, Python, tmux and the GitHub command-line tool, and noted that the agent runs with full access as the operating-system user, so it advised isolating it before use.

Citing a Chinese tech outlet's account of DeepSeek's report, MarkTechPost said that in a simulation with about 300 messages per run, about 20 of them real work requests, the super-agent reached a 95th-percentile task completion time of 15.7 minutes, against 29.5 minutes for a single-session agent with subagents. MarkTechPost noted that these figures are self-reported, came from tests with synthetic messages and simulated tools, and that real coding quality was not measured.

image.alt: GitHub preview card for the deepseek-ai/dsh-superagent-prototype repository

stories.title: NVIDIA releases Auto Ontology, an open-source layer meant to help AI agents query company data using trusted business definitions
paragraphs: MarkTechPost reported on Nov. 1, 2026 that NVIDIA has released Auto Ontology, an open library under the Apache 2.0 license. NVIDIA's GitHub page describes it as a library that builds a context layer from enterprise metadata, telling AI agents where data lives, what it means, whether and how to use it, and where it came from, and that serves this layer to any agent harness through MCP, a command-line tool and an API.

NVIDIA's repository states the motivation directly: "a revenue metric answered faster is worth nothing if the number is wrong." According to the repository, the library generates ontologies from metadata, reconciles inconsistent definitions across systems, checks generated queries against certified definitions and returns provenance with every answer. MarkTechPost reports that NVIDIA's developer page frames the output as a starting ontology that business experts still test, refine and certify.

The repository lists four core services: a Next.js web front end, a FastAPI back end using LangChain, an ingestion worker that writes embeddings, and Postgres with pgvector. MarkTechPost reports that source databases can be Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake or DuckDB, and that the MCP server offers nine read-only tools with no tool for browsing raw schemas, which the outlet says NVIDIA chose on purpose so agents reach data through the semantic layer. By default it uses NVIDIA NIM endpoints with Nemotron models, according to the repository.

NVIDIA also publishes a separate evaluation harness, auto-ontology-eval, which compares a schema-only model against the ontology-grounded agent on benchmarks including BIRD, MarkTechPost reports. The outlet notes that the harness repository lists limitations, including that optional examples are given only to the ontology arm, so a gain measured with them reflects those inputs and not grounding alone.
